location: the Spanish kingdoms (Valencia, Andalusia, Aragon, Catalonia, Castile, Murcia); embarkation for North Africa and other destinations

date.note: A consulta of the Council of State of 4 April 1609 set the process in motion (Benítez Sánchez-Blanco). Philip III's letter of 4 August 1609 was published in Valencia by the viceroy, the Marquis of Caracena, with the bando of 22 September 1609 ordering the Moriscos of that kingdom to embark for North Africa. The marquis of San Germán was commissioned in November 1609 to expel the Moriscos of Andalusia, Murcia, and Hornachos, and that edict was published in Seville on 17 January 1610 (Boeglin); the expulsions from Aragon, Catalonia, and Castile followed in 1610, and they are dated here only to the year because the exact dates of those decrees were not confirmed in a scholarly source consulted. The last operations, including the valley of Ricote in Murcia, fell in 1613-1614, and a decision of 19 February 1614 ended the search for those not expelled (Benítez Sánchez-Blanco). Al-Maqqari dates the expulsion to 1017 AH, which Gayangos converts as 'A.D. 1610'; 1017 AH in fact ran from April 1608 to April 1609, before the Valencian bando.

summary: The Expulsion of the Moriscos was the removal, by royal orders issued from 1609 (Valencia) through 1610 and enforced until 1614, of the baptized descendants of Iberia's Muslims from the Spanish kingdoms, most of them shipped to North Africa. Henri Lapeyre counted nearly 275,000 people expelled, and the publisher's description of a major collective study gives about 300,000; the motives (religious unity, fear of a Moroccan or Ottoman invasion supported by a Morisco rising, the policy of the Duke of Lerma's government) and the completeness of the expulsion are debated by historians.
description:
By 1609 the Moriscos, baptized Muslims and their descendants, had lived as nominal or sincere Christians for three or four generations. The process, as Rafael Benítez Sánchez-Blanco describes it, was set in motion by a consulta of the Council of State of 4 April 1609 answering a threat, held to be certain, of a Moroccan invasion with Dutch support that a Morisco rising would back, and he describes a government determined to 'limpiar' the Monarchy's domains of Morisco blood. The decision for Valencia is stated in Philip III's letter of 4 August 1609 to the viceroy, reproduced in the bando the viceroy published on 22 September. In the king's own voice, the letter recalls the long efforts to convert the Moriscos of Valencia and Castile, the edicts of grace, and the measures to instruct them, and 'lo poco que todo ello ha aprovechado'; it reports that 'muchos y muy doctos y santos hombres' had urged him to act, and that a junta in Valencia including 'el Patriarca' (the archbishop Juan de Ribera) had considered whether expulsion could be avoided; and it gives as decisive his having learned 'por avisos ciertos y verdaderos' that the Moriscos, 'continuando su apostasía y prodición', sought 'por medio de sus embajadores y por otros caminos el daño y perturbación de nuestros reinos'. On that stated ground the king resolved 'que se saquen todos los moriscos de ese reino, y que se echen en Berbería'. This entry reports these grounds as the decree's own attributed justification, not as findings about the Moriscos.

The bando gave the Moriscos of Valencia, men, women, and children, three days from its publication in their localities to leave for the ports of embarkation, carrying such movable goods as they could on their persons, on pain of death. Any person might, without penalty, seize and rob ('prenderle y desbalijarle') a Morisco found outside his locality after the three days, deliver him to the nearest justice, and kill him if he resisted. The same bando provided that they be landed in Berbería 'sin que reciban mal tratamiento, ni molestia en sus personas', that no Old Christian or soldier 'sea osado a tratar mal de obra ni de palabra' any Morisco, and that anyone hiding them or helping them evade departure incur 'pena de seis años de galeras'. Their remaining property was granted to their lords, and destroying it was made a capital offence for the whole locality. Six households in every hundred, chosen among the oldest farmers who had given most signs of being Christians, were to stay 'para que se conserven las casas, ingenios de azúcar, cosechas de arroz, y los regadíos, y puedan dar noticia á los nuevos pobladores'. Further exemptions covered children under four whose parents consented, the children under six of Old Christian fathers together with their Morisca mothers, those who had lived among Christians for two years without attending the meetings of the aljamas, and those admitted to communion with their prelates' licence; ten Moriscos from the first sailing were to be allowed back to report that the passage was safe, and those who wished to go to other kingdoms might do so 'sin entrar por ninguno de los de España'. Embarkations from Valencia began that autumn, and risings in two districts, La Marina and the Muela de Cortes, were suppressed. The expulsion was then extended to Andalusia, Murcia, and Hornachos (the edict was published in Seville on 17 January 1610) and, during 1610, to Aragon, Catalonia, and Castile, including the Granadan Moriscos dispersed through Castile after 1571 and the 'antiguos', in Benítez Sánchez-Blanco's definition 'mudéjares castellanos convertidos masivamente a principios del siglo XVI'; royal commissioners pursued those who evaded or returned, the last Murcian communities of the valley of Ricote being expelled in 1613-1614.

The numbers rest chiefly on Henri Lapeyre's reconstruction from official records, which counted nearly 275,000 expelled, as Benítez Sánchez-Blanco cites it; the publisher's description of the García-Arenal and Wiegers volume gives about 300,000 persons affected. How complete the expulsion was is contested. Lapeyre estimated, as Michel Boeglin reports, that some 10,000 to 15,000 people remained or returned in the peninsula. Trevor Dadson, in his 2007 study of the Old Moriscos of Villarrubia de los Ojos and in later work, argues that many assimilated Moriscos resisted expulsion or returned and were reabsorbed; Benítez Sánchez-Blanco, engaging the 2007 study, documents many forms of return and of resistance, in which towns, bishops, and lords sometimes pressed to keep their Moriscos (as in Plasencia and the county of Oropesa, and in the count of Salinas's clash with the commissioners over Ricote), but resists generalizing the Villarrubia case and judges that the Morisco 'nation' ceased to exist as communities, at once in Spain and within some generations in North Africa.

On motives, historians weigh the security fears recorded in the Council of State's deliberations and invoked in the royal letter; the religious arguments of churchmen such as Ribera, whose campaign to persuade the king Benjamin Ehlers traces; and the politics of Philip III's favourite, the Duke of Lerma, whose government Antonio Feros studies. The publisher's description of the García-Arenal and Wiegers volume frames the expulsion as legitimized by an ideology of religious and political unity. Christian opinion was not uniform: Benítez Sánchez-Blanco describes two opposed intellectual positions at the start of the seventeenth century, that of the humanist Pedro de Valencia, whose Tratado acerca de los moriscos de España argued for the Moriscos' full integration, so that the very name of Morisco would disappear, and that of Ribera, who urged expulsion and warned in a memorial of 1602 of the spread of 'mala sangre morisca'. Contemporary Spanish apologists defended the expulsion in print, among them the Dominicans Jaime Bleda (Corónica de los moros de España, 1618) and Damián Fonseca (Justa expulsión de los moriscos de España, 1612), whose works are recorded here as attributed positions of the expelling side, not as evidence of what the Moriscos believed.

The Maghribi Muslim view of the event is recorded in the closing part of the narrative quoted in al-Maqqari's Nafh al-tib, which reaches the time of al-Maqqari himself (d. 1041/1632, born in Tlemcen and then living in Fez) and reports that the expulsion 'took place in our times, in the year 1017 of the Hijra'. It states that many thousands of the exiles went to Fez and thousands by way of Oran to Tlemcen, while 'the greater part took the road to Tunis'; that 'few, however, reached the place of their destination; for they were assailed on the road by the Arabs and such as fear not God, and they were plundered and ill-treated, especially on the road to Fez and Telemsán', whereas most of those bound for Tunis arrived safely and settled its towns and districts; that others settled in Tetouan, Salé, and the plain of the Mitidja near Algiers, the sultan of Morocco establishing a body of them at Salé, 'where they have since made themselves famous by their maritime expeditions against the enemy of God'; and that a few went to Istanbul, Egypt, and Syria. A narrative in a Morisco's own voice survives in the Kitab Nasir al-din (completed in Cairo in 1637) of Ahmad ibn Qasim al-Hajari, from Hornachos, secretary to the Sa'did sultans of Morocco, an account of his travels and of his religious disputations with Christians and Jews. The settlement of the exiles across the Maghrib and the Ottoman lands, and their memory of al-Andalus, are the subject of the second part of the García-Arenal and Wiegers volume.
editorial_notes: HOME TRADITION (ADR-0010): filed under islam because the entry chiefly concerns the expelled community, baptized Christians of Muslim descent whose religious identity was at the centre of the decision; this is a storage convention, not a claim of ownership. VOICES: the Christian state and Church side is sourced from its own texts (the royal letter and bando; Pedro de Valencia; the apologists Bleda and Fonseca) and from historians, and is shown as divided (Pedro de Valencia against Ribera; towns, bishops, and lords who sought to keep Moriscos). The passage in al-Maqqari is the closing part of the narrative he quotes, which reaches his own time ('in our times', 1017 AH); it is treated as a contemporary Maghribi Muslim voice, not a Morisco voice; the only Morisco-own voice cited is al-Hajari, whose work was verified to exist but not read and is rated medium. NEUTRALITY: the decree's grounds (apostasy, treason, foreign contacts) are quoted and attributed to the royal letter, not asserted; the apologists are recorded only as attributed positions (neutrality #11); numbers and motives are attributed to the historians who advance them, and the dispute over the completeness of the expulsion (Dadson against Benítez Sánchez-Blanco) is presented without adjudication (neutrality #2). No claim is made about the expulsion's economic effects beyond the bando's own provision for retaining cultivators, quoted in its words. The compares_with link to the 1492 expulsion of the Jews states the shared question and the difference and rests on scholarship that makes the comparison (Benítez Sánchez-Blanco 2013, p. 473), per ADR-0005. DATES: see the date note; the per-kingdom decree dates for Aragon, Catalonia, and Castile are given at year level because they were not confirmed in a scholarly source consulted; Gayangos's conversion of al-Maqqari's 1017 AH as A.D. 1610 is recorded alongside the corrected range. SOURCING (neutrality #8, #9): (a) modern historians (Harvey; García-Arenal and Wiegers; Lapeyre; Dadson; Benítez Sánchez-Blanco; Boeglin; Ehlers; Feros); (b) primary texts of the expelling side (the 1609 royal letter and bando in Janer's 1857 edition; Pedro de Valencia; Bleda; Fonseca) and of the Muslim side (al-Maqqari; al-Hajari). No encyclopedias or tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE: the bando was read line by line in Janer's printed edition (archive.org scan), which is the source of the transcription hosted by Yale's Iberian Connections project, and is rated high; al-Maqqari (vol. 2, p. 392 in Gayangos), Benítez Sánchez-Blanco's paper, and Boeglin's article were read directly for the passages used and are rated high. Pedro de Valencia's Tratado, Bleda, and Fonseca were verified to exist (the Tratado's modern editions through Benítez Sánchez-Blanco's note; Bleda and Fonseca through digitized copies and catalog records) but not read, and are rated medium; the other monographs were verified to exist and be on-topic through publisher, catalog, and review records but not read line by line, and are rated medium.

relations.note: The Morisco community expelled in 1609-1614 was created by the forced conversions that followed the breach of the Capitulations of Granada (1499-1502) and, in the Crown of Aragon, the conversions of 1525-1526.
The decrees of 1609-1614 expelled the Moriscos, the baptized Muslims of the Spanish kingdoms and their descendants.
The exiles were the last descendants in Iberia of the Muslim population of al-Andalus; in North Africa they were often known as Andalusians.

Compares the question, not the answer, per neutrality principle #10. Both are expulsions of a religious minority ordered by the Spanish Crown on grounds that included protecting the Catholic faith, and historians of the Moriscos draw the comparison: Rafael Benítez Sánchez-Blanco, writing on the fate of the expelled Moriscos as communities, observes that 'la comparación con los judíos expulsados y con los judeoconversos puede ser ilustrativa'. They differ in whom they targeted and what they left open: the decree of 1492 expelled professing Jews and left baptism as the alternative to exile, whereas the decrees of 1609-1614 expelled baptized Christians of Muslim descent, whom the royal letter treated as apostates, with exemptions only for limited categories such as those judged to live as Christians.

The expulsion figures in debates over coexistence in early modern Spain: Trevor Dadson argues from the Old Moriscos of Villarrubia that coexistence and assimilation were real and that many escaped expulsion or returned, while Rafael Benítez Sánchez-Blanco resists generalizing that case and holds that the Moriscos ceased to exist as communities after the expulsion.

sources.citation: Philip III, letter to the Marquis of Caracena (4 August 1609), and Bando de la expulsión de los moriscos del reino de Valencia, published at Valencia, 22 September 1609. In Florencio Janer, Condición social de los moriscos de España: causas de su expulsión, y consecuencias que esta produjo en el orden económico y político. Madrid: Imprenta de la Real Academia de la Historia, 1857, documentos, no. XCVIII, pp. 300-303 ('según se conserva en el folio 34 de la Mano 50 de Mandamientos y embargos de la corte civil de Valencia del año 1611'). Read line by line in the archive.org scan: the king's stated grounds ('lo poco que todo ello ha aprovechado'; 'muchos y muy doctos y santos hombres'; 'por avisos ciertos y verdaderos'; 'continuando su apostasía y prodición'; 'por medio de sus embajadores y por otros caminos el daño y perturbación de nuestros reinos'; 'que se saquen todos los moriscos de ese reino, y que se echen en Berbería') and the bando's thirteen articles (three days to leave; art. 2, seizure, robbery, and killing of those found outside their localities; property to the lords; art. 5, six households in a hundred to remain; art. 9, children under four; art. 10, children under six of Old Christian fathers; arts. 11-12, exemptions; art. 8, ten to return and report; art. 13, departure to other kingdoms). A transcription of the same text, reading 'Barbería', is hosted by Yale University's Iberian Connections project. The primary-text lens of the expelling authority.
sources.license: Public domain (1609 document; 1857 edition). Read line by line for the passages cited.

sources.citation: al-Maqqari, Ahmad ibn Muhammad. Nafh al-tib min ghusn al-Andalus al-ratib, partially translated as The History of the Mohammedan Dynasties in Spain, trans. Pascual de Gayangos. 2 vols. London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1840-1843. Vol. 2, Book VIII, ch. 7, pp. 391-392: the closing part of the narrative quoted by al-Maqqari (d. 1041/1632), which reaches his own time, on the secret practice of Islam after the conversions and on the expulsion, 'an event which took place in our times, in the year 1017 of the Hijra' (converted by Gayangos as A.D. 1610), with the destinations of the exiles (Fez; Tlemcen by way of Oran; 'the greater part' to Tunis; Tetouan, Salé, the Mitidja; a few to Istanbul, Egypt, and Syria) and the attacks on those travelling to Fez and Tlemcen ('Few, however, reached the place of their destination'). The Maghribi Muslim primary-text lens; the passages used were read directly in the public-domain scan.

sources.citation: Benítez Sánchez-Blanco, Rafael. 'Continuidad de la presencia morisca en España después de las expulsiones: resistencias a la expulsión, permanencias y retornos de los moriscos.' In Actas del XII Simposio Internacional de Mudejarismo (Teruel, 14-16 de septiembre de 2011), 473-490. Teruel: Centro de Estudios Mudéjares, Instituto de Estudios Turolenses, 2013. Scholarly paper read directly for: the comparison with 'los judíos expulsados y con los judeoconversos' and the disappearance of the Morisco 'nation' (p. 473); the consulta of the Council of State of 4 April 1609 and the threat of a Moroccan invasion with Dutch support (p. 475); the risings in La Marina and the Muela de Cortes (p. 479); towns, bishops, and lords pressing to keep Moriscos (pp. 474, 481); the definition of the 'antiguos' as 'mudéjares castellanos convertidos masivamente a principios del siglo XVI' (p. 480); Lapeyre's count of 'cerca de 275.000 expulsados' (p. 482, citing Lapeyre, Spanish ed. 2009, pp. 218-220); Ricote in 1613 (pp. 483-484); his disagreement with Dadson's 2007 Villarrubia thesis (pp. 474, 489); and the decision of 19 February 1614 and the opposed positions of Pedro de Valencia and Juan de Ribera (p. 490). Open-access PDF hosted by the Instituto de Estudios Turolenses.

Peer-reviewed article on the expulsion from Andalusia, Murcia, and Hornachos under the marquis of San Germán, commissioned in November 1609, with the edict published in Seville on 17 January 1610, the second and third expulsions, and Lapeyre's estimate of 10,000-15,000 who remained or returned. sources.citation: García-Arenal, Mercedes, and Gerard Wiegers, eds. The Expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain: A Mediterranean Diaspora, trans. Consuelo López-Morillas and Martin Beagles. The Medieval and Early Modern Iberian World 56. Leiden: Brill, 2014. ISBN 978-90-04-25920-1. doi:10.1163/9789004279353. Translated from Los moriscos: expulsión y diáspora (Valencia, 2013). Part one treats the decision to expel, its context, and the roles of the Vatican and the religious orders; part two treats the diaspora, including the Moriscos in Tunisia, routes and financing, and polemical writings in exile, comparing it with that of the Jewish conversos; the publisher's description, reproduced in the BnF catalog summary, describes the expulsion as having 'affected about 300,000 persons'. The outside-scholarship lens. Verified to exist and be on-topic (BnF catalog record and summary; University of Amsterdam and other repository chapter records), not read line-by-line.
